summary.prose: Adds one daemon method, repo.buildDefaults.migrate, that the user runs once after updating the daemon. It walks the registered repos in order, calls the existing applyBuildDefaults for each, and returns every repo's outcome with counts per outcome, so repos registered before the add-time defaults get their project type's typical build commands. It never overwrites existing commands and a failure on one repo never stops the others. Nothing runs by itself, and no client button is added.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Standalone feature — no parent HLD. Design directly against the repo, grounded on the s1 analyze passes. There are no HLD shared contracts to honour.

api.name: migrateBuildDefaults
api.signature: migrateBuildDefaults(repos: readonly string[], deps?: { readonly configPath?: string; readonly writeKeys?: typeof writeRepoEntryKeys }): Promise<BuildMigrationReport>

parameters.name: repos
parameters.purpose: The registered repo paths, exactly as the registry holds them, in registry order.

parameters.name: deps
parameters.purpose: The same test seams applyBuildDefaults takes, passed through to it.

returns.meaning: One entry per repo, in the order given, each holding that repo's BuildDefaultsOutcome, plus how many repos had each outcome.

errors.condition: applyBuildDefaults never throws and reports a failure as { applied: false, reason: 'write-failed', note }; this function runs the repos one at a time and records each result, so one repo's failure does not stop the rest.

preconditions: repos holds registered repo paths; the caller (the RPC method) reads them from the registry.
postconditions: Every repo whose own github.json entry set none of typecheckCommand, testCommand and resultFormat, and whose project type has typical commands, now has all three, written in one write.
No entry that set any of the three keys was changed.
A second call with the same repos changes nothing and reports already-set for the repos the first call set.

api.name: repo.buildDefaults.migrate
api.signature: 'repo.buildDefaults.migrate': (params: unknown) => Promise<BuildMigrationReport | { ok: false; error: { code: 'registry-unreadable'; message: string } }>

parameters.name: params
parameters.purpose: None are read; the method acts on every registered repo.

returns.type: BuildMigrationReport | { ok: false; error: { code: 'registry-unreadable'; message: string } }
returns.meaning: The report, or a business error as data when the registry cannot be listed.

errors.condition: listRepos throws; returned as data, nothing is written.

preconditions: The daemon is running and its registry is readable.
postconditions: The result is the report of migrateBuildDefaults over the registered repos as listed by listRepos at the time of the call.
Nothing is written under any repository; only ~/.insrc/github.json, through the daemon's own writer.

api.name: applyBuildDefaults
api.signature: applyBuildDefaults(repoPath: string, deps?: { readonly configPath?: string; readonly writeKeys?: typeof writeRepoEntryKeys }): Promise<BuildDefaultsOutcome>

parameters.name: repoPath
parameters.purpose: The repo to apply the defaults to.

parameters.name: deps
parameters.purpose: Test seams for the config path and the writer.

returns.meaning: applied with the project type, or not applied with the reason.

errors.condition: Any failure is { applied: false, reason: 'write-failed', note }.

postconditions: Unchanged by this Story: it is consumed as is, and still the only thing that decides whether to write.

dataModelChanges.details: { readonly ok: true; readonly repos: readonly BuildMigrationEntry[]; readonly counts: { readonly applied: number; readonly 'already-set': number; readonly 'node-default': number; readonly 'no-typical-commands': number; readonly 'write-failed': number } }. Read-only result of one migration run; not stored anywhere. counts has a key for every outcome, 0 when none, so a client can print it without checking for missing keys. The sum of the counts equals repos.length.
{ readonly repo: string; readonly outcome: BuildDefaultsOutcome } where repo is the path as the registry holds it. One per registered repo, in registry order.

The type is unchanged. Its meaning gains a second producer: it is now returned either from repo.add (as buildDefaults) or per repo from the migration. The reasons stay already-set, node-default, no-typical-commands and write-failed, so the clients and docs that read them are unaffected.

errorCases.detection: listRepos(db) in the method's handler rejects (the registry store is unreadable).
errorCases.response: Return { ok: false, error: { code: 'registry-unreadable', message } } as data; no repo is touched and nothing is written.
errorCases.userImpact: The call reports why nothing was migrated; the daemon stays up.

errorCases.scenario: ~/.insrc/github.json exists but cannot be read or is malformed.
errorCases.detection: readRepoEntry returns not-ok inside applyBuildDefaults for each repo.
errorCases.response: Every repo's entry reports { applied: false, reason: 'write-failed', note } carrying the read error, and the file is left exactly as it is.
errorCases.userImpact: The report shows write-failed for every repo with the file's error; counts.write-failed equals the number of repos. Fixing the file and running again migrates them.

errorCases.scenario: The write for one repo is refused or throws (disk full, file changed by another process on every attempt, permission).
errorCases.detection: writeKeys returns not-ok or rejects inside applyBuildDefaults, which catches both.
errorCases.response: That repo reports write-failed with the note; the loop continues with the next repo; no lone command is left because the three keys are one write.
errorCases.userImpact: The report names the repo that failed; the others are migrated. Running again retries only the repos that still have none of the keys.

errorCases.scenario: The client disconnects or the daemon stops part-way through the loop.
errorCases.detection: The socket closes or the process exits between two repos.
errorCases.response: Repos already written keep their commands (each write is atomic); the rest are untouched; no state records a half-run.
errorCases.userImpact: A second call migrates the remainder and reports already-set for the first ones.

edgeCases.expected: { ok: true, repos: [], counts: all zero }.

edgeCases.input: A registered repo's directory no longer exists on disk.
edgeCases.expected: Its project type reads as unknown, so it reports no-typical-commands and nothing is written.

edgeCases.input: A Node repo, or a repo whose root holds markers of two types.
edgeCases.expected: node-default for Node, no-typical-commands for the mixed or unknown root; no write for either.

edgeCases.input: A repo whose entry sets only one of typecheckCommand, typecheckCommand or resultFormat, including a lone command the gate would refuse.
edgeCases.expected: already-set; the entry is not changed, so a bad stored value is left for the user to fix, not overwritten.

edgeCases.input: The method is called twice in a row, or two calls overlap, or repo.settings.set runs during a call.
edgeCases.expected: Writes go through the daemon's single serialised writer; the second call reports already-set for repos the first set; a user's own set is never overwritten because applyBuildDefaults re-reads the entry before it writes.

edgeCases.input: A repo whose commands the user deliberately cleared with repo.settings.set null, then the method is run again.
edgeCases.expected: It is treated as unset and gets the defaults again, because nothing records a clear; this is a property of running the method by hand and is stated in the docs.

invariantsToPreserve.text: applyBuildDefaults never overwrites an entry that sets any of the three keys, writes them in one write, and never throws; the migration adds no second place that decides whether to write.
repo.add is unchanged: it stays the only automatic caller of applyBuildDefaults and its reply keeps carrying buildDefaults.
The registry is walked with the daemon's listRepos in src/db/repos.ts, not the CLI service's function of the same name.
The new method writes only ~/.insrc/github.json through the daemon's writer and nothing under any user repository, so its repo-call audit entry is daemon-store, as repo.add's is.
repo.settings.get and the build phase still write nothing and resolve a repo's commands as before; the migration adds no write to a read path.
Every existing method keeps its row in the handler tables, the thread routing table, the repo-call audit and the recorded method list; only the new method is added to each.

migration.stateBefore: Today applyBuildDefaults (src/daemon/repo-settings.ts:201-223) is called only from the repo.add handler in buildHandlerRuntime (src/daemon/handler-runtime.ts) and from tests, so a repo registered before it has none of typecheckCommand, testCommand and resultFormat in its own entry of ~/.insrc/github.json. Registered repos are listed by listRepos in src/db/repos.ts:226-235. No method walks every registered repo to apply the defaults, so each old repo needs the 'Use suggested build commands' action by hand.
migration.stateAfter: A daemon method, repo.buildDefaults.migrate, walks the registered repos in order and calls applyBuildDefaults for each, returning one outcome per repo and counts per outcome. After the user runs it once, every old Python, Go, Rust and JVM repo that had none of the three keys has them; repos that set any key, Node repos and unknown repos are unchanged. The method is in the handler tables, the thread routing table, the repo-call audit and the recorded method list, and in docs/daemon.md. repo.add, repo.settings.get and the build phase behave as before.

migrationSteps.action: The user updates the daemon so it carries repo.buildDefaults.migrate (and the add-time defaults); the method does nothing until called.

The user calls repo.buildDefaults.migrate once; for each registered repo with none of the three keys and a type with typical commands, the daemon writes the three keys in one write to that repo's entry of ~/.insrc/github.json and reports applied; every other repo is left as it is and reports why.

The user reads the report; a repo that shows write-failed is retried by calling the method again after the cause is fixed, and a wrong default is edited or cleared with repo.settings.set, in the Repo Configuration page, or by the 'Use suggested build commands' action.

migration.backwardCompat: No existing method, payload or client changes: repo.add keeps its reply, repo.settings.get and repo.settings.set keep theirs, and the build phase reads the commands as before. The new method is purely additive, so a client that does not know it is unaffected, and an older daemon answers 'unknown method' for it. The data written is the same three keys the add-time defaults and the 'Use suggested' action already write, so github.json gains no new shape. A rollback is clearing the three keys of a repo with repo.settings.set null, which the daemon already supports; note that running the method again applies the defaults again to a repo whose keys were cleared.

alternativesConsidered.name: One on-demand daemon method
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: A single daemon method, run by the user after updating, applies the defaults to every registered repo and returns each repo's outcome.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add one daemon RPC method (repo.buildDefaults.migrate) with no required params. It lists the registered repos (listRepos in src/db/repos.ts), calls the existing applyBuildDefaults(repoPath) for each one in turn, and returns { repos: [{ repo, outcome }] } using the existing BuildDefaultsOutcome, plus counts per outcome. Because applyBuildDefaults already refuses to overwrite, writes the three keys in one write and never throws, the method inherits those rules and is idempotent: a second run reports already-set. The method is added to the handler tables, the thread routing table, the repo-call audit (a daemon-store entry: it writes ~/.insrc/github.json, not files of a repo) and the recorded method list, and documented in docs/daemon.md. Nothing runs by itself.
pros: The smallest change that fully meets the Story: one loop over two existing functions.
The user chooses when it runs and sees exactly what each repo got, including write-failed.
No new persistent state, no startup ordering, no surprise writes to ~/.insrc/github.json.
Reuses applyBuildDefaults's never-overwrite, one-write and never-throw rules unchanged.
cons: It has to be run by hand once; a repo registered by an old client and never migrated stays without commands until then.
Needs a way to call it: any IPC client can, but no terminal or IDE button is added by this Story.

alternativesConsidered.name: Run automatically at every daemon start
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: At startup the daemon applies the defaults to every registered repo that has none, with no method and no manual step.
alternativesConsidered.approach: In the daemon's startup, after the registry is available (where src/daemon/index.ts already hands the registered repos to the tracker refresh hooks), loop over the registered repos and call applyBuildDefaults for each, logging each outcome through the daemon logger. There is no IPC method, so no registry entries for a method, and the user does nothing beyond updating the daemon.
pros: Nothing to remember: every old repo is covered the first time the updated daemon starts.
No new IPC surface, so no method-table, routing or audit entries.
cons: It runs on every start, not once: a repo whose commands the user deliberately cleared gets the defaults written back at the next start, because applyBuildDefaults treats a repo with none of the keys as unset.
The user sees no result except log lines, so a write-failed repo is easy to miss.
A write to ~/.insrc/github.json happens during startup, where a slow or failing file write is harder to see and to test.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Re-applies defaults after a deliberate clear and gives the user no report; it also takes the timing out of the user's hands.

alternativesConsidered.name: On-demand method plus a once-only run at start
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: The a1 method, and the daemon also runs it once automatically at start, remembering that it did with a marker.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Do a1, and at daemon start call the same function once, then write a small marker in the daemon's state directory (a file or key) recording the migration as done so later starts skip it. The method stays for a manual or repeated run.
pros: Covers old repos without a manual step and runs only once, so a later deliberate clear is not overwritten at the next start.
Keeps the on-demand method for repos registered later by an old client.
cons: Adds persistent state (the marker) and a startup step with failure handling: what to record when some repos failed, and whether to retry them at the next start.
Two entry points for one behaviour, each needing tests, and the marker's storage location and format to design and document.
More than the Story asked for: the user said they would run the migration themselves after updating.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Adds persistent state and a second entry point for behaviour the user said they would run themselves.

alternativesConsidered.name: Apply lazily the first time a repo's settings are read
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: repo.settings.get, or the build phase, applies the defaults the first time it finds a repo with none.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Make the read of a repo's build settings (repo.settings.get, or the build step's profile resolution) call applyBuildDefaults when the repo has none of the three keys, so every repo migrates the first time anyone looks at it. There is no migration method and no loop.
pros: No separate action and no startup work; repos migrate as they are used.
Only repos that are actually used are touched.
cons: A read that writes: repo.settings.get is defined and tested as writing nothing, and the build gate resolves its commands once at the start of a phase, so a hidden write there would change what a build runs mid-flight.
The same deliberate-clear problem as a2: clearing the keys is read as 'unset' and the defaults come back.
Timing is unpredictable and the user gets no report of what changed.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: A read that writes breaks the contract of repo.settings.get and can change a build's commands mid-phase; ranked above a2 and a3 only for its small size.

sbdry4 note: the edge case that says a user's own repo.settings.set during a call is never overwritten is too strong. applyBuildDefaults reads the entry and then writes, as separate steps, so a set landing between the two can be overwritten; the window is the same as at repo.add and the build must document it rather than claim it away.
